focus: /æ/ (bad, hat) vs /e/ (bed) · /ɔː/ (tall, short) vs /ɒ/ (hot) · question-word stress (WHAT, WHERE) · /ɜː/ (girl, shirt) vs /ɔː/ (short) · adjective + noun stress and linking
focus_ar: /æ/ مقابل /e/، و /ɔː/ مقابل /ɒ/، ونبر أدوات السؤال، و /ɜː/ مقابل /ɔː/، ونبر الصفة مع الاسم
arabic_challenge: Arabic has no /æ/, /e/ distinction of this kind and no /ɜː/ at all, so 'bad/bed' and 'girl/goal' collapse. Question words also carry heavy stress in English — flattening them makes questions hard to follow.

isolation.instructions: /æ/ (bad, hat, black) = mouth WIDE open, tongue flat and low at the front. /e/ (bed, red, best) = mouth half open, tongue a little higher. This pair changes meaning constantly.
isolation.instructions_ar: /æ/ الفم مفتوح واسع واللسان مسطح تحت. /e/ الفم نص مفتوح واللسان أعلى شوية. الفرق بيغيّر المعنى كثير.

sentence_practice: The red bed is very big.
daily_drills.record_this: He is a handsome man and he is very friendly. That black hat is bad, but the red bed is the best.
daily_drills.self_check: Say 'bad' then 'bed'. Put a finger on your chin — it should drop lower for 'bad'.

isolation.instructions: /ɔː/ (tall, short, all, four) = LONG, lips firmly rounded and pushed forward. /ɒ/ (hot, not, long) = SHORT, lips only lightly rounded.
isolation.instructions_ar: /ɔː/ طويل والشفاه مدوّرة بقوة للأمام. /ɒ/ قصير والشفاه مدوّرة بخفة.

sentence_practice: He is tall and she is short.
daily_drills.record_this: He is tall and she is short. All four boxes are small. It is not very hot today, so I want more water before I walk.
daily_drills.self_check: Say 'caught' then 'cot'. The first must be noticeably longer with tighter lips.

isolation.instructions: English questions put strong stress on the question word AND on the key content word: 'WHAT is he LIKE?' 'WHERE is your HOUSE?' The little words between them stay weak.
isolation.instructions_ar: الأسئلة الإنجليزية النبر فيها على أداة السؤال وعلى الكلمة المهمة: 'WHAT is he LIKE?'. والكلمات الصغيرة بينهم تبقى خفيفة.

daily_drills.record_this: What is he like? Where is the tall man? What colour is your new car? Who is that friendly woman?
daily_drills.self_check: Clap on the stressed words only. Two claps per question — the question word and the key word.

isolation.instructions: /ɜː/ (girl, shirt, first, work) = tongue in the MIDDLE, lips NEUTRAL (not rounded) — a long, flat 'er'. /ɔː/ (short, four) = lips ROUNDED. Arabic has neither, so the lips decide it.
isolation.instructions_ar: /ɜː/ اللسان في النص والشفاه محايدة (مش مدوّرة) — صوت 'إر' طويل مسطح. /ɔː/ الشفاه مدوّرة. الشفاه هي الفيصل.

sentence_practice: The girl wears a short shirt.
Her first birthday is in the morning.
daily_drills.record_this: The girl is wearing a short shirt. Her first birthday is tomorrow morning. I work early and then I walk to the small shop.
daily_drills.self_check: In a mirror, say 'shirt' — your lips must stay flat. Then 'short' — they must round.

isolation.instructions: When you describe something, BOTH the adjective and the noun usually carry stress, and they link smoothly: a BLACK CAR, a TALL MAN, a BIG OLD HOUSE. Comparatives end weakly: TALL-er, BIGG-er (the -er is a tiny /ə/).
isolation.instructions_ar: في الوصف، الصفة والاسم الاتنين منبورين وبيتوصّلوا: a BLACK CAR. والمقارنة نهايتها خفيفة: TALL-er.

sentence_practice: She has a beautiful new car.
He is taller than his brother.
daily_drills.record_this: She has a beautiful new car. He is taller than his brother, and that old house is much bigger than mine.
daily_drills.self_check: Say 'taller'. Is the ending a light /ə/, not a strong 'ERR'?

challenge_sentences: WHAT is he LIKE? He is tall and friendly.
The girl has a short red shirt.
That black hat is bad, but the bed is very good.
He is taller than all four men.
daily_drills.record_this: What is he like? He is tall, handsome and very friendly. The girl has a short red shirt. That black hat is bad, but the bed is good. He is taller than all four men.
daily_drills.self_check: Check the lips: flat for /ɜː/ (shirt, work), rounded for /ɔː/ (short, walk).

test_yourself.instructions: Record yourself describing people and things. Then listen back and check each sound group.
test_yourself.instructions_ar: سجّل نفسك وانت توصف أشخاص وأشياء، وبعدين اسمع وراجع كل مجموعة أصوات.
test_yourself.passage: What is your brother like? He is tall and handsome, and he is very friendly. He always wears a black shirt and a red hat. My sister is shorter than him, and she has long hair. Where do they work? They work in a big old building near the small shop. What colour is your car? It is white, and it is bigger than my old one. All four of us are happy.

sounds_to_check./æ/ vs /e/: black, hat, handsome, has — red, bed, very, friendly, seven
sounds_to_check./ɔː/ vs /ɒ/: tall, all, four, short, more — hot, not, long, shop, got
sounds_to_check./ɜː/ vs /ɔː/: shirt, work, girl, first, her — short, four, more, walk
sounds_to_check.question-word stress: WHAT is he LIKE?  WHERE do they WORK?  WHAT COLOUR is it?
sounds_to_check.adjective + noun: a BLACK SHIRT, a BIG OLD BUILDING, TALL-er, SHORT-er

scoring_guide.90_100: 'bad/bed' and 'shirt/short' are clearly distinct and questions are well stressed. Ready for week 9.
scoring_guide.70_89: Good; /ɜː/ occasionally drifts toward a rounded vowel.
scoring_guide.50_69: 'bad/bed' still merges, or questions sound flat. Repeat days 1 and 3.
scoring_guide.below_50: Redo days 1-5 with the mirror, watching lip rounding carefully.

for_arabic_speakers: /æ/ vs /e/ (bad/bed) is one of the highest-frequency meaning-changing pairs in English. Widen the mouth for /æ/.
/ɜː/ (shirt, work) needs FLAT lips. If you round them you will say 'short' instead.
Question-word stress is what makes a question sound like a question, alongside intonation.
supplementary_notes.recording_requirement: Record the 'record_this' line daily; compare day 7 with day 1.
